It was Pauls afternoon to appear before the faculty of the Pittsburgh High School to account for his various misdemeanors, for he had been suspended a week before. <break time="0.8s" /> He entered the room smiling, and although his clothes were a trifle outgrown, there was something of the dandy about him, for he wore a red carnation in his buttonhole. <break time="0.8s" /> The faculty felt that this red flower was not at all suited to the contrite spirit that befitted a boy who had been sent home in disgrace. <break time="0.8s" /> When questioned by the principal, Paul stated, politely enough, that he wanted to come back to school, though this was a lie, for he found lying indispensable for overcoming friction. <break time="0.8s" /> His teachers were asked to state their charges against him, which they did with such rancor and aggrievedness as showed that this was not a usual case. <break time="0.8s" /> Disorder and impertinence were among the offenses named, yet each instructor felt that the real cause of the trouble lay in the boys hysterically defiant manner and his open contempt. <break time="0.8s" /> Paul stood through it all smiling, his pale lips parted over his white teeth, and he used his eyes in a conscious, theatrical way, peculiarly offensive in a boy. <break time="0.8s" /> Afterward the drawing master voiced the feeling of them all when he declared that there was something wrong about the fellow, something that none of them understood. <break time="0.8s" /> He had once seen Paul asleep at his desk, and he remembered with a shock how old and tired the boys white face had looked, as if something were haunting him.

Paul was an usher at Carnegie Hall, and on concert nights he always arrived early, wandering through the picture gallery before the doors opened to the public. <break time="0.8s" /> Once he had put on his uniform, which was one of the few that at all approached fitting, Paul became vivacious and animated, and he felt like a different person. <break time="0.8s" /> He was a model usher, running up and down the aisles with gracious smiles, as though it were a great reception and he were the host of the evening. <break time="0.8s" /> When the symphony began, Paul sank into one of the rear seats with a long sigh of relief, and the first notes seemed to free some hilarious spirit within him. <break time="0.8s" /> It struggled there like the Genius in the bottle found by the Arab fisherman, and as the lights danced before his eyes, the hall blazed into unimaginable splendor. <break time="0.8s" /> It was not that symphonies, as such, meant anything in particular to Paul, but the music carried him away from everything that was dull and ugly in his life. <break time="0.8s" /> After one concert, Paul followed the German soloist to her hotel and stood outside in the rain, watching the doors open and close upon a world of warmth and light. <break time="0.8s" /> He longed to enter that fairy world, but when the cold rain soaked his clothes, he wondered whether he was destined always to shiver in the black night outside.

Paul always dreaded going home to Cordelia Street, where all the houses were exactly alike and businessmen of moderate means raised large families and sent their children to Sunday school. <break time="0.8s" /> He hated the ugly yellow wallpaper of his room, the pictures of George Washington and John Calvin above his bed, and the whole flavor of an ordinary, respectable life. <break time="0.8s" /> That night he could not face his father, so he crept in through a basement window and sat awake until dawn, half afraid that his father would mistake him for a burglar. <break time="0.8s" /> On Sunday afternoons all the people of Cordelia Street sat out on their front steps, and the men talked about prices, promotions, and the legends of the iron kings. <break time="0.8s" /> Pauls father held up as a model a young clerk who worked for a steel magnate and who, on his employers advice, had married early and settled down. <break time="0.8s" /> Paul cared only for the tales of the iron kings, with their palaces in Venice and yachts on the Mediterranean, for the clerks dull virtues meant nothing to him. <break time="0.8s" /> That evening he asked his father for carfare, saying he was going to study geometry with a classmate, and his father gave him the money, warning him not to be out late. <break time="0.8s" /> But Paul went instead to the theater, where his friend Charley Edwards, a young actor in the stock company, let him help in the dressing room and watch the rehearsals.

In New York he bought fine clothes, silk underwear, and silver mounted brushes, and he took rooms at the Waldorf, explaining that he was from Washington and that his parents were abroad. <break time="0.8s" /> Surrounded by flowers, soft carpets, and music drifting up from the dining room, he felt that this was exactly what all the struggle of his life had been about. <break time="0.8s" /> One night he went out with a wild boy from San Francisco, a freshman at Yale, and they stayed out until dawn, but in the morning they parted singularly cool. <break time="0.8s" /> He felt no remorse, for here, as he glanced down at his dress coat, he was sure that it would be impossible for anyone to humiliate him. <break time="0.8s" /> On the eighth morning he found his own story in a Pittsburgh paper, which reported that his father had repaid the money and was coming to New York to bring him home. <break time="0.8s" /> The gray monotony of Cordelia Street stretched before him in hopeless, unrelieved years of Sunday school, yellow wallpaper, and damp dish towels, and he could not bear it. <break time="0.8s" /> He left the city and wandered out into the snowy country beside the railroad, where the red carnations in his coat had already drooped and lost their glory in the cold. <break time="0.8s" /> It seemed to him that the flowers had had only one splendid breath, for all their brave mockery at the winter, and he buried one of them gently in the snow. <break time="0.8s" /> When the train came near through the falling snow, Paul stepped toward it, and there Cather ends his story, letting him drop back into the immense design of things.
